sections.label: Content note
sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses abuse, forced treatment, restraint and deaths in psychiatric hospitals. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: What this page covers
sections.heading: What this page covers
sections.body:
This page covers psychiatric hospitals and psych wards for adults and young people, whether or not a hospital is also part of the troubled teen industry, and how they connect to it. Many youth programs we track sit on a psychiatric hospital's campus, carry its name and its owner, or are a unit inside it. Those programs are in [our directory](/tti-program-index/). Psychiatric units and other providers outside the industry that use its practices or refer young people to it are on our [list of mental health providers](/mental-health-providers/).

The teen programs are the psychiatric hospitals' business. The same companies own both, the teen program grew out of the hospital, and both are run the same way: people who cannot leave are kept to fill paid beds, and they are held down to control them.

We are not the experts on psychiatric hospitals. The organizations listed below are, and many of them are run by people who have been hospitalized themselves.

sections.label: The same owners
sections.heading: The same owners
sections.body:
The two largest for-profit owners of psychiatric hospitals, Universal Health Services (UHS) and Acadia Healthcare, both run youth programs. UHS has more of them in our records than any other company.

Table: The two largest for-profit chains
| | UHS | Acadia |
|---|---|---|
| Behavioral health facilities, end of 2025 | 182 in the U.S., 161 in the U.K., 3 in Puerto Rico[^1] | 277 in 40 states and Puerto Rico, over 12,500 beds[^2] |
| Youth programs in our records | [75](/operator/universal-health-services/) | [14](/operator/acadia-healthcare/) |

On the ground the hospital and the teen program often sit side by side. UHS's list of its own facilities puts psychiatric hospitals beside Provo Canyon School and Copper Hills Youth Center in Utah and Oak Plains Academy in Tennessee. Some share a name and a city: Cedar Ridge Behavioral Hospital and Cedar Ridge Residential Treatment Center in Oklahoma City, and North Star Hospital in Anchorage with the North Star DeBarr and Palmer residential treatment centers.[^1] About 60 programs in our records, under many owners, are named for a hospital or one of its units, such as Cedar Crest Hospital & RTC in Texas, Hampstead Hospital & RTC in New Hampshire and West Oaks Hospital PRTF in Texas.[^3]

The chains bought their way into teen programs. Charter Behavioral Health Systems bought the original campus of Provo Canyon School in 1986, and by 1999 ran 91 hospitals treating 35,000 children and adolescents a year.[^4] When Charter went bankrupt in 2000, UHS bought 11 of its facilities, Provo Canyon School among them.[^5][^6] UHS added the Keystone youth programs and five former Brown Schools programs in 2005, and Acadia bought CRC Health Group, owner of Aspen Education Group's teen programs, in 2015.[^4]

People and patients crossed over too. In 1993 Robert Lichfield, who started as a dorm parent at Provo Canyon School and went on to found WWASP, took over the management of Brightway Adolescent Hospital in St. George, Utah. Health officials said the hospital promptly began sending young people to tough-love behavior programs.[^7]

sections.label: Born in the hospital
sections.heading: Born in the hospital
sections.body: The teen program's form and its methods both came out of psychiatry. The residential treatment center began as a psychiatric clinic's children's division, the Menninger Clinic's Southard School, in 1926.[^8] The group confrontation used on teenagers came from the same place. Synanon grew out of its founder's part in an LSD study funded by the National Institute of Mental Health. The psychiatrist Daniel Casriel co-founded Daytop Village in 1964 with an NIMH grant, and the psychiatrist Gerald Davidson co-founded Elan School in 1971. The Seed, CEDU and Straight, Inc. carried the same methods to teenagers across the country.[^9]

sections.label: Held for pay
sections.heading: Held for pay
sections.body:
A teenager in a residential program cannot walk out, and neither can many psychiatric patients. The teenager is held because a parent or a state placed them. An adult can be held against their will too: every state lets a person be held for an emergency evaluation and lets a court order a longer commitment.[^10]

Every day a patient stays is a day the hospital is paid for, so a stay can last as long as someone pays. At UHS, 175 current and former staff interviewed by BuzzFeed News in 2016 described pressure to fill beds and to keep patients until their insurance ran out. UHS rejected the allegations.[^11] At Acadia, more than 50 current and former executives and staff told The New York Times in 2024 that the company held patients against their will when it was not medically necessary, often for financial reasons. In at least 12 of the 19 states where Acadia runs psychiatric hospitals, patients, employees and police officers had alerted authorities.[^12]

The Senate Finance Committee found the same business in the companies' youth programs. Its 2024 investigation of youth residential treatment run by UHS, Acadia, Devereux and Vivant found that these providers "optimize per diems by filling large facilities to capacity and maximize profit by concurrently reducing the number and quality of staff" ([our summary](/warehouses-of-neglect/)).[^13]

The public pays for the extra days. Medicaid and Medicare paid 72 percent of Acadia's 2025 revenue.[^2] That is why the federal government's cases against both chains were about billing. In 2020 UHS paid $122 million to settle False Claims Act allegations that from 2006 to 2018 its behavioral health facilities admitted patients who did not need inpatient care, kept them longer than needed, understaffed, and improperly used physical and chemical restraints and seclusion. Liability was not determined.[^14] In 2024 Acadia paid $19.9 million, admitting no liability, to settle a federal investigation of medical necessity, admissions, discharges and length of stay at several of its facilities.[^2] It has since received grand jury subpoenas from the Justice Department's Criminal Division about the admissions, length of stay and billing of its acute psychiatric hospitals. As of July 2026 those investigations were open and no findings had been made.[^15]

sections.label: Held down
sections.heading: Held down
sections.body:
The same restraint has killed people in hospitals and teen programs alike. In 1998 the Hartford Courant's series "Deadly Restraint" counted 142 deaths tied to restraint or seclusion over ten years in psychiatric hospitals and wards, group homes and youth residential facilities.[^16] The next year *60 Minutes II* opened its report on Charter, then the owner of Provo Canyon School, with Tristan Sovern, 16, asphyxiated while staff restrained him at a Charter hospital in Greensboro, North Carolina. He was the third patient in four months to die in restraints at a Charter hospital.[^17]

The rules came only after the deaths, and hospitals did not follow them. Until 1999 no federal rule governed restraint and seclusion in psychiatric hospitals.[^16] The rules written since forbid restraint or seclusion "imposed as a means of coercion, discipline, convenience, or retaliation by staff," count a drug given to manage behavior outside standard treatment as a restraint, and require hospitals to report to CMS every death in restraint or seclusion.[^18] Between August 1999 and December 2004 hospitals failed to report 44 of 104 documented deaths.[^19]

The practice goes on in the companies' youth programs. In 2024, asked whether a child could be chemically restrained and secluded at once, UHS personnel told Senate Finance Committee staff "there are no rules preventing doubling or tripling up on a restraint and seclusion," a practice federal regulations prohibit.[^13]

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If someone is in danger now**, call 911. For a mental health crisis, call or text [988](tel:988), the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, 24 hours a day.
- **Protection and Advocacy agency.** Every state and territory has one. Under the federal PAIMI program they investigate abuse, neglect and rights violations against people with mental illness in public and private facilities, including restraint and seclusion.[^20] Find yours in [NDRN's directory](https://www.ndrn.org/about/ndrn-member-agencies/).
- **State health department.** Hospitals are licensed by the state, and the state survey agency investigates complaints for Medicare and Medicaid. CMS lists [each state's complaint contact](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/health-safety-standards/quality-safety-oversight-general-information/contact-information).
- **The Joint Commission**, if the hospital is accredited by it: [report a safety concern online](https://www.jointcommission.org/en-us/contact-us/report-a-patient-safety-event) or call 1-800-994-6610. You can report anonymously.
- **A death in restraint or seclusion** must be reported by the hospital to CMS. You can also tell the state survey agency and the Protection and Advocacy agency yourself.
- For troubled teen programs, including youth residential treatment run by the same companies, use [our reporting directory](/report-abuse/).

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [MindFreedom International](https://mindfreedom.org/): A human rights organization in mental health care, with psychiatric survivors among its board and past leaders. It works against forced psychiatric treatment.
- [National Association for Rights Protection and Advocacy (NARPA)](https://www.narpa.org/): Supports people with psychiatric diagnoses in exercising their legal and human rights, and works to end forced treatment.
- [National Empowerment Center](https://power2u.org/): Works with people with lived experience of mental health issues, trauma and extreme states. It keeps directories of peer respites and peer-run warmlines.
- [Wildflower Alliance](https://wildfloweralliance.org/): A grassroots group in Western Massachusetts and online offering peer support, advocacy and training, including peer-run respites.
- [National Disability Rights Network (NDRN)](https://www.ndrn.org/): The national organization of the Protection and Advocacy agencies, the largest providers of legal advocacy for people with disabilities.
- [Bazelon Center for Mental Health Law](https://www.bazelon.org/): A national legal advocacy organization for the civil rights of people with mental disabilities, through lawsuits and policy work.
- [Mad in America](https://www.madinamerica.com/): A publication of the Mad in America Foundation with research news, original journalism and writing by people with lived experience of psychiatric care.

sections.label: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.heading: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.body: If you have been hospitalized, work in psychiatric care or advocate in this field, and something on this page is wrong or missing, please [tell us](/contact/). We will change it.
